summary: A revision of the File Transfer Protocol from RFC 172. It adds two new file transfer requests, new error codes and editorial clarifications, then restates the protocol. FTP is a user-level protocol for moving files between ARPANET hosts. It was updated by several RFCs and replaced by RFC 354.

eli5.summary: The rules for copying files from one computer to another across the network, rewritten with a few extra commands and error messages.

subtitle: A 1971 revision of the ARPANET file transfer protocol, with new requests, new error codes and a fixed opcode list.

tldr.problem: Users on the ARPANET needed a standard way to move files between host computers and to use the storage of remote hosts without writing special code for each one.
tldr.mechanism: FTP sends short control transactions, each starting with an opcode byte, over the Data Transfer Protocol of RFC 264. A user connects to socket 3 on the serving host and sends requests such as retrieve, store, append, delete or list.
tldr.outcome: This RFC revises RFC 172 by adding two requests and two error codes. It was itself updated by RFC 281, RFC 294 and RFC 310 and obsoleted by RFC 354.

today: RFC 265 is obsoleted by RFC 354 and was updated by RFC 281, RFC 294 and RFC 310, so it is a stage in the early history of FTP, not the current text.

sections.title: What FTP Is For
sections.content:
The file transfer protocol (FTP) is a user-level protocol for moving files between host computers on the ARPANET. Its goals are to promote sharing of files, to encourage implicit use of computers without an explicit login, and to shield the user from the different file and storage systems of different hosts.

This paper revises RFC 172 and then restates the whole protocol. The changes are two new file transfer requests, new opcode assignments, two new error codes ('incorrect or missing identifier' and 'file already exists') and editorial clarifications. FTP relies on the Data Transfer Protocol of RFC 264 to carry its data.
sections.eli5: FTP is a way to borrow and send files between computers that have different ways of storing them. This paper is the fixed-up second edition of the rules.

sections.title: Files, Pathnames and Access
sections.content:
A file is an ordered set of arbitrary length, identified by its pathname. FTP provides standard file commands but no standard naming convention, so each user must follow the naming convention of the file system being used. Pathnames are sent in network ASCII.

FTP does not restrict what a file holds. A 'set data type' transaction can say how data is structured, using a data type code and optionally a byte size. The standard default is to assume nothing and treat the data as a bit stream with a byte size of 1. A host must accept data even if it does not recognize the type.

Access control is left to the serving file system. FTP only carries username and password identifiers, which are normally sent at the start of a connection and are neither acknowledged nor allowed to be acknowledged.
sections.eli5: A file is just a bunch of data with an address, and the sender can add a note saying what kind of stuff it is. A name and password can be shown at the door, but the other computer decides who gets in.

sections.title: Requests and Their Order
sections.content:
The user side opens the connection and sends the request. The server side listens on socket 3, the standard preassigned socket, and complies. Each control transaction starts with an opcode byte, from 00 (set data type) up to 0D (acknowledge). Opcodes hex 5A through FF are for experimental use.

The requests are retrieve, create (error if the file exists), store (replace if it exists), append (error if the file does not exist), append with create, delete, rename from and rename to, and list. The store request carries a 4-byte 'allocate size' field before the pathname. A rename from request must always be followed by a rename to request.

After a retrieve or list, the server sends the data and an end-of-file indication. After create, store, append or append with create, the user sends the data and end-of-file, and the server must acknowledge. Delete and rename are also acknowledged. Either host may abort at any time with an error terminate or by closing the connection.
sections.eli5: You knock on door number 3, say what you want (get, save, add, delete or rename a file), and the other computer does it. For saving, it says thanks when it is done. Either side can stop at any time.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
An error terminate carries an error code in its second byte, and an ASCII message may follow with any code. With code 0A the text is required. The codes cover a system error outside the protocol, name syntax errors, access control violations, a user abort, allocate size problems, improper transaction order, an opcode not implemented, a failed file search, an incorrect or missing identifier and a file that already exists in a create request.

The errors relate to file transfer only. Data synchronization errors are left to the data transfer level. No completion codes are defined for acknowledge.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the computer sends a numbered note saying what, such as 'no such file' or 'wrong password'.

items.label: Set data type
items.desc: Identifies the structure of the data that follows.

items.label: Retrieve
items.desc: Copy a file from server to user.

items.label: Create
items.desc: Write a file; error if it already exists.

items.label: Store
items.desc: Write a file; replace it if it exists.

items.label: Append
items.desc: Add to an existing file; error if missing.

items.label: Append with create
items.desc: Add to a file, creating it if needed.

items.label: List
items.desc: Send a directory list or file information.
